analysis.one_liner: Bans spread pricing in Medicaid and forces pharmacy benefit managers to disclose and pass through drug-price gains in Medicare.
analysis.headline: Introduced December 4, 2025 with 27 bipartisan cosponsors, the bill has sat in the Senate Finance Committee with no action since its same-day referral.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill targets pharmacy benefit managers (PBMs) — the middlemen that negotiate drug coverage for insurers and employers. It would ban "spread pricing" in Medicaid, where a PBM charges the state more than it pays the pharmacy and keeps the difference, and require PBMs in Medicare's drug program to be paid flat service fees rather than keeping rebates, discounts, and fees tied to drug prices. It would also let any willing pharmacy join Medicare drug-plan networks, publish government survey data on what pharmacies actually pay for drugs, and require detailed annual PBM disclosure of revenues, affiliate steering, and rebate deals.
analysis.who_benefits: Independent and community pharmacies, especially rural ones, gain fairer reimbursement and new ways to challenge abusive plan contracts. Medicare and Medicaid beneficiaries and taxpayers gain from eliminated spread pricing and clearer pricing data. The federal government gains new enforcement tools, funded with roughly $336 million in fiscal 2026 appropriations across CMS, the HHS Inspector General, and MedPAC [S2].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Independent pharmacies and Medicare and Medicaid patients

how_it_helps.text: Bans spread pricing in Medicaid: contracts must pay pharmacies only ingredient cost plus a dispensing fee at least equal to what the state would pay directly, pass the full amount through to the pharmacy, limit the middleman to a fair-market-value administrative fee, and disallow any spread from being claimed as federal match [S2].

Expands the federal survey of what pharmacies actually pay for drugs (NADAC) to include mail-order and specialty pharmacies, publishes the results monthly, and lets the HHS Inspector General study how PBM- and wholesaler-affiliated pharmacies report costs, with civil penalties up to $100,000 per violation for pharmacies that refuse to report or give false data [S2].

Requires Medicare drug plans to accept any willing pharmacy that meets standard contract terms, directs the Secretary to set standards for reasonable contract terms, and creates a confidential process for pharmacies to file complaints — with anti-retaliation protections and civil monetary penalties for plans or PBMs that violate the standards [S2].

Starting in 2028, PBMs in Medicare Part D may derive income only from bona fide flat service fees: no payments contingent on drug price, rebate volume, or formulary placement; rebates negotiated with manufacturers must be fully passed through to the plan; and violators must disgorge the money [S2].

Forces PBMs to file detailed annual reports on drugs dispensed, reimbursement by dispensing channel, revenue retained by the PBM and its affiliates, steering of patients toward PBM-owned pharmacies, and formulary choices that favor brand drugs over covered generics — and gives plans audit rights over their PBMs [S2].
Orders a Government Accountability Office study of price-based fee structures across the drug supply chain and MedPAC reports on PBM agreements, aimed at informing further legislation [S2].

analysis.who_pays: PBMs and their insurer parents (CVS, Cigna, UnitedHealth are the largest) bear the direct cost: lost spread-pricing revenue, lost rebate and fee retention in Medicare, disgorgement, audit exposure, and compliance with extensive reporting. Taxpayers fund about $336 million in fiscal 2026 appropriations ($188 million and $113 million to CMS, $20 million and $5 million to the HHS Inspector General, $9 million a year for the drug price survey, $1 million to MedPAC) [S2]. Plan sponsors face compliance costs that could nudge premiums.
analysis.who_pays_short: PBMs, their insurer parents, and federal taxpayers

drawbacks.text: The Medicare PBM reforms apply only to Part D plans and Medicare Advantage drug coverage, not to commercial insurance or employer plans, so most working-age Americans' coverage stays untouched [S2].

Key parts are slow: the drug-price survey does not cover mail-order and specialty pharmacies until 18 months after enactment, and the Medicaid pass-through rules and Medicare PBM fee and transparency requirements do not apply until 2028 [S2].

The bill adds reporting burdens for pharmacies and plan sponsors, backed by civil money penalties of up to $100,000 per violation for pharmacies that fail to respond to price surveys, and $188 million in new CMS implementation funding whose cost lands on taxpayers [S2].

The 340B carve-out lets hospitals and covered entities be paid above a drug's actual acquisition cost, with only annual aggregate reporting, a compromise that leaves a known pricing dispute unresolved [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core trade is real money for a small group against transparency and pricing reform for two of the largest public health programs. The Medicaid spread-pricing ban and the Part D fee restrictions strike directly at the PBM business model's least defensible features, and the pharmacy survey data gives regulators and the public a baseline they have lacked for mail and specialty drugs. The weaknesses are scope (no commercial market coverage) and pace (most provisions wait until 2028), which lets the current revenue model run for years before the restrictions bite. It is a genuine reform bill whose main design concession is the 340B carve-out and whose main cost is a few hundred million dollars in implementation funding against potentially much larger program savings.

outcome.mechanism: Introduced and referred to the Senate Finance Committee on December 4, 2025; no committee action, vote, or floor action has occurred yet.

narrative.text: Senator Mike Crapo introduced the bill on December 4, 2025, joined by 21 original cosponsors including both Senate party leadership figures on health policy [S1][S2].
The same day, the Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Finance, which has jurisdiction over Medicare and Medicaid [S4].
Cosponsorship grew to 27 members, split 12 Democrats and 15 Republicans, giving the bill broad bipartisan support but no committee or floor action since referral [S3].
As of the end of the available record, the bill's only actions are introduction and referral; no markup, hearing, or vote is listed [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No one yet has won or lost on the merits: the bill is alive but has not moved. If it stalls, the beneficiaries will be the pharmacy benefit managers whose Medicaid spread pricing and Medicare rebate and fee retention would otherwise end.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Nobody yet — the bill awaits committee action

against.name: Pharmacy benefit managers (CVS Caremark, Express Scripts, Optum Rx) and their trade association
against.what_they_did: No direct action on this bill appears in the record; the industry has historically lobbied against federal spread-pricing bans and fee restrictions, which would cut their core revenue

sides.party_line_note: All 27 cosponsors span both parties — 12 Democrats and 15 Republicans — with the two leaders of the Senate Finance Committee from opposite parties as the lead backers [S3].

industries.industry: Pharmacy benefit managers (CVS Caremark, Express Scripts, Optum Rx)
industries.note: The bill bans the spread-pricing revenue PBMs collect in Medicaid, restricts their Medicare Part D income to flat service fees, forces full pass-through of manufacturer rebates, requires disgorgement of prohibited remuneration, and exposes their affiliate steering to public reporting. Their profits come from opaque pricing intermediation, which is exactly what the bill strips out.

industries.industry: Independent and community pharmacies, especially rural
industries.note: Pharmacies gain pass-through reimbursement in Medicaid instead of having the spread skimmed, accurate government benchmarks that for the first time cover mail and specialty competitors, an any-willing-pharmacy right in Medicare drug plans, and a confidential complaint process with anti-retaliation protection against plan and PBM contract abuses.

industries.industry: Health insurers and Medicare drug plan sponsors
industries.note: Plan sponsors gain the right to audit their PBMs, collect disgorgement from them, and be reimbursed for penalties caused by PBM failures; they lose pricing flexibility in Medicaid contracts and any-willing-pharmacy leverage over pharmacy networks. Because the largest insurers own the largest PBMs, the PBM-side losses fall on the same parent companies.

Manufacturers must disclose contracts that tie rebates on one drug to formulary placement or utilization management on others, and plans must justify covering a brand drug while leaving a marketed generic off the formulary — disclosure that threatens rebate-wall strategies, though the bill imposes no direct price controls on them.

industries.industry: Mail-order and specialty pharmacies (largely PBM- and insurer-affiliated)
industries.note: These pharmacies are brought under the federal acquisition-cost survey for the first time, and their owners must report what share of prescriptions they capture and how much they charge versus unaffiliated pharmacies, ending a long-standing data blind spot that favored affiliated dispensing.

analysis.trajectory: The bill sits with the Senate Finance Committee, whose chair and ranking member both sponsored it, so a committee markup in 2026 is plausible; a close predecessor package of PBM reforms cleared the same committee in a prior Congress but never received a full Senate vote. With 27 bipartisan cosponsors and no floor action scheduled, the realistic path is committee consideration followed by an uncertain attempt to attach the provisions to a larger year-end health or spending package, since free-standing floor time for such bills is rare.
